The Story of Sukomal Muni

I bow to the supremely pure Lord Jina, by merely remembering whose name one can attain all manner of wealth and prosperity, and I write the story of Sukomal Muni.

This story is from the time when Atibal was king of Kaushambi. There lived a priest named Somsharma. His wife was Kashyapi. They had two sons, Agnibhut and Vayubhut. Being overly indulged by their parents, they could not study properly. And truly, without merit, knowledge does not come to anyone. By the strange workings of time, Somsharma died prematurely. The two brothers were then mere fools. Seeing their foolishness, King Atibal gave the priestly position — which should have been theirs — to someone else. Truly, fools are honoured nowhere.

Seeing themselves insulted, the two brothers were deeply grieved. Then some sense returned to them. They now thought of studying. They went to their uncle Suryamitra in Rajgriha and told him their whole story. Seeing their desire to learn, Suryamitra began teaching them himself, and within a few years, he made them fine scholars. When they became learned, they returned to their city and demonstrated their knowledge to King Atibal. The king, pleased to see them as scholars, restored their father's priestly position to them. Truly, through the grace of Saraswati, nothing is impossible in this world.

One evening, Suryamitra was offering water to the setting sun. On his finger was a valuable jewelled ring belonging to the king. While offering water, the ring slipped off his finger and fell into the pond below the palace. By fortune, it landed in a blooming lotus. When the sun set, the lotus closed, and the ring was trapped inside. When Suryamitra finished his worship and looked at his finger, he realised the ring was gone. His fear knew no bounds. What would he answer when the king asked for the ring? He searched everywhere but could find no trace. Then, on someone's advice, he went to the clairvoyant monk Sudharm and, with joined hands, asked, "Lord, please tell me where the ring is."

The monk, through his clairvoyance, saw the ring in the lotus and told Suryamitra. The ring was recovered, and Suryamitra was overjoyed. He asked the monk, "How is it that you can see things so far away, while we cannot see even what is right before us?" The monk replied, "Through the practice of dharma, the soul's natural power of knowledge is unveiled. Ordinary beings see only with physical eyes, which are limited. But those who purify the soul through right faith, knowledge, and conduct attain clairvoyance and even omniscience."

Hearing this, Suryamitra was deeply impressed. He developed faith in Jain dharma and eventually took initiation as a monk. His nephew Sukomal too became a great monk. Through intense austerity and meditation, Sukomal destroyed his karmas and attained liberation.

This story teaches that knowledge and spiritual power come through merit and the practice of dharma. The two foolish brothers, through their own effort, became scholars. And through the monk's teaching, they learned that true knowledge — the knowledge of the soul — comes only through spiritual practice. The wise should cultivate both worldly learning and spiritual wisdom.
